We consider polynomial equations, or systems of polynomial equations, with integer coefficients, modulo prime numbers $p$.
We offer an elementary approach based on a counting method. The outcome is a weak form of the Lang-Weil lower bound
for the number of solutions modulo $p$, only differing from Lang-Weil by an asymptotic $p^\epsilon$ multiplicative factor.
Our second contribution is a reduction lemma  to the case of a single equation which we use to extend our results
to systems of equations. We show further
how to use this reduction to prove the full Lang-Weil estimate for varieties, assuming it for hy\-per\-sur\-faces,
in a version using a variant of the classical degree in the error term.
Let $F(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ be a nonconstant polynomial in one or several variables and with integer coefficients.
For which prime numbers $p$ the equation:
has integer solutions? and for such primes $p$, what is the size of the set of solutions? These are the questions that
we consider, for such an equation, and more generally for a system of several such polynomial equations. In geometric terms,
the problem is to count the number of rational points over finite fields $\Ff_p$ on the zero set $Z(F\bmod p)$, or, for a system,
on the zero set of an ideal generated by several polynomials, regarded modulo $p$.
A classical and deep achievement in this perspective is the

\textbf{\textit{Lang-Weil estimate}} \cite{LW}. \emph{Given nonnegative integers $d$, $r$, $h$, there is a positive constant $A(r,h)$ such that for every finite field $\Ff_q$ of cardinality $q=p^\beta$ with $p$ prime and $\beta\geq 1$, and every prime ideal $I\subset \Ff_q[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ such that the affine variety $V=Z(I) \subset \Aa^r$ is geometrically irreducible\footnote{i.e.{} irreducible after scalar extension to $\overline{\Ff_q}$.}, of dimension $\dim(V) = d$ and of degree ${\rm deg}(V) = h$, we have:
Here $\dim(V)$ is the dimension of $V$ and $\deg(V)$ is its degree, i.e.{} the number of intersection points of $V$ with $\dim(V)$ hyperplanes in general position.
For a single equation $F(x_1,\ldots,x_r) = 0$, i.e.{} when $V$ is a hypersurface, $\dim(V)=r-1$ and $\deg(V) = \deg(F)$.

We will use the following bounds for  $c_p(F)$ as landmarks.
An upper bound is easily provided by the Zippel-Schwartz lemma, which is a several variable generalization of the fact that over a field, a one variable nonzero polynomial has no more roots
than its degree; see Section \ref{sec:Zippel-Schwartz} for a reminder.
\textbf{\textit{Zippel-Schwartz upper bound.}} \emph{For all primes $p$ we have $c_p(F) \leq \deg(F) \, p^{r-1}$.}

A second contribution of this paper is a reduction lemma to a single equation for a system of several polynomial equations, i.e.{} in geometric terms, from the case of a general affine variety to that of

a hypersurface. The notation $c_p(I)$ used below for an ideal $I\subset \Zz[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ generalizes $c_p(F)$: for every $p\in \mathcal{P}$, $c_p(I)$ is the number of points $\ul \omega \in \Ff_p^r$ such that $(P \bmod p)(\ul \omega) = 0 \bmod p$ for every $P\in I$; that is: $c_p(I) = \card(Z(I\bmod p)(\Ff_p))$ \footnote{that is: the set of $\Ff_p$-rational points on the Zariski-closed subset $Z(I\bmod p)\subset \Aa_{\Ff_p}^r$.}.
Let $I\subset \Zz[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ be a prime ideal such that $I\cap \Zz = \{0\}$. Set $V=Z(I) \subset \Aa^r$ and $d=\dim(V)$.

The classical approach to Lang-Weil goes by induction, on the dimension of $V$, using Chow varieties \cite{LW}. With Lemma \ref{thm:reduction-intro} we can work instead
with the number of defining equations of $V$, reducing to the case it is one, i.e.{} $V$ is an hypersurface $H: F(\ul t, y)=0 \subset \Aa^{d+1}$.
Other approaches proceed as we do and construct  hypersurfaces $H \subset \Aa^{d+1}$
from general affine varieties $V\subset \Aa^r$. But while these
use generic linear projections $\Aa^r \rightarrow \Aa^{d+1}$ and try to optimize them
to birationally map $V$ to a good hypersurface $H$,
we directly construct a spe\-cific hypersurface $H$ that \emph{locally represents $V$},
in the sense of Definition \ref{def:def_hyp}. Furthermore, our construction
is performed over rings. See Lemmas \ref{lem:exist_rep_hyp}--\ref{lem:main}, which rest on the Noether normalization lemma and
the primitive element theorem and do not use Chow varieties.
We give two applications. The first one extends Theorem \ref{th:onepoly} to systems of equations.
Let $I\subset \Zz[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ be an ideal such that $I\cap \Zz = \{0\}$ (not necessarily prime). Then the series $\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} \frac{c_p(I)}{p^{d+1}}$ is divergent.
That is: Theorem \ref{th:onepoly} holds with $c_p(I)$ and $d+1$ replacing $c_p(F)$ and $r$.
This first application includes further a generalization of the {\emph{Zippel-Schwartz upper bound} for $c_p(I)$ with $\deg(F)$ replaced by some constant $M$
The second application is a proof, assuming the case of hypersurfaces, of the \emph{Lang-Weil es\-timate} itself, with the following
difference concerning the error term. Instead of the degree $\deg(V)$, we introduce the \emph{hypersurface degree} $\hdeg(V)$ of

Using a more general form of Lemma \ref{thm:reduction-intro} (namely Lemma \ref{lem:main}), we prove the following statement,
assuming the case  of hypersurfaces (which is well-known; see e.g.{} \cite{cafure-matera}).
The \emph{Lang-Weil estimate} holds with the condition $\deg(V)= h$ replaced by the condition $\hdeg(V)= h$. \footnote{Corollary \ref{cor:cons2-intro}
is explicitly restated in Section \ref{sec:severalpoly}, when it is proved.}
If $V$ is a hypersurface, then  it follows from the definitions that $\hdeg(V) \leq \deg(V)$, but it is not clear
to us how degree and hypersurface degree compare in general. The hypersurface degree seems however a more intrinsic notion than the usual degree (Remark \ref{rem:on-hyp-deg}).
Section \ref{sec:onepoly} is devoted to the case of one polynomial equation. Theorem \ref{th:onepoly} is proved.

Section \ref{sec:severalpoly} is concerned with the case of systems of polynomial equations: Lemma \ref{lem:main}, which generalizes Lemma \ref{thm:reduction-intro}, is proved; then we deduce Corollary \ref{cor:cons1-intro} and Corollary \ref{cor:cons2-intro}; a final illustration is given in Section \ref{ssec:ostrowski}.
This section is aimed at proving Theorem \ref{th:onepoly}. The proof is divided into three stages which correspond to Sections
\S \ref{ssec:zero-density}--\ref{ssec:end-proof}.  The preliminary Section \ref{sec:Zippel-Schwartz} is a reminder on the Zippel-Schwartz lemma.
Our proposed approach is elementary. As a comparison,

\subsection{Second stage of the proof of Theorem \ref{th:onepoly}}
We prove the density formula from Lemma \ref{lem:new-lemma} below,
by adjusting a method going back to Ekedahl and Poonen \cite{Poo}, \cite{Ek}.
For $M\ge0$, let $\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\le M}$ be the set of all $\ul x \in \Zz^r$ such that the only prime divisors of $F(\ul x)$
are $> M$ or are in the set $\mathcal{F}$ of fixed prime divisors, that is:
First we compute the density of $\mathcal{Q}_{p}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{p}$ for any fixed prime $p\in \mathcal{P}$.
Note that $p$ divides $F(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ with $(x_1,\ldots,x_r) \in \Zz^r$ if and only if $p$ divides $F(x_1+k_1p,\ldots,x_r+k_rp)$ for any $(k_1,\ldots,k_r)\in\Zz^r$.
Hence $\mathcal{Q}_{p}$ is invariant by any translation of vector in $(p\Zz)^r$.
Hence, as a function of $B$, the cardinality $\card (\mathcal{Q}_{p} \cap \llbracket 0,B-1 \rrbracket^r)$ is asymptotic to $c_p \cdot \left( \frac B p \right)^r$ as $B\rightarrow \infty$.
Note further that if $p$ is a fixed prime divisor then $\mu(\mathcal{Q}_p)=1$ and $\mu(\mathcal{R}_p)=0$.

Next fix $M\ge0$ and let $\{p_1,\ldots,p_\ell\} = (\mathcal{P} \setminus\mathcal{F}) \cap \llbracket 0,M \rrbracket$ be the set of primes $\le M$ that are not fixed prime divisors, and let $N$ be the product of these primes.

The density is indeed positive: the series $\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}} \frac{c_p}{p^r}$ converges and any factor of this infinite product is nonzero because $c_p=p^r$ if and only if $p$ is a fixed prime divisor (which is ruled out by $p\notin \mathcal{F}$).
The second part of Theorem \ref{th:onepoly} is an immediate consequence of the first one.
As a comparison with our approach, we explain how to use the \emph{Lang-Weil estimate} to deduce the \emph{Lang-Weil lower bound} (both as stated in Section \ref{sec:motivation}).
The argument, in addition to the \emph{Lang-Weil estimate}, uses the Chebotarev density theorem and the Ostrowski theorem; recall however that the resulting
bound is better than that of Theorem \ref{th:onepoly}. Remark \ref{rem:lagarias-odlyzko} completes the argument to obtain the full Theorem \ref{th:onepoly}, i.e.{} the divergence
of the series $\sum_{p\in \mathcal{P}} c_p(F)/p^r$, but at the cost of using the Lagarias-Odlyzko effective form of the Chebotarev theorem.
Let $F \in \Zz[\ul x]$ be a nonconstant polynomial in $r\geq 1$ variables.
Let $P \in \overline \Qq[\underline x]$ be an irreducible factor of $F$ in the UFD $\overline \Qq[\ul x]$.

Let $K$ be a number field containing all coefficients of $P$, and $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$, $\beta \neq 0$, such that $\tilde P =\beta P \in \mathcal{O}_K[\ul x]$ (with $\mathcal{O}_K$ the ring of integers of $K$).
It follows from the Chebotarev density theorem that the set $S_K$ of primes $p$ that are totally
split in $K$ is of density $\gamma \ge 1/n_K!$, where $n_K = [K:\Qq]$. In particular, $S_K$ is infinite.

Remove from $S_K$ the finite set of primes $p$ for which $\beta$ is in a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $K$ above $p$. Denote the resulting set by $S_K^\prime$. For every prime  $p\in S_K^\prime$, select a prime $\mathfrak{p}$ of $K$ above $p$. By definition of $S_K$, we have $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p} \simeq \Ff_p$. By the Ostrowski theorem, for all but finitely many $p\in S_K^\prime$, the reduced polynomial $(\tilde P  \bmod \mathfrak{p}) \in \Ff_p[\ul x]$ is irreducible in $\overline{\Ff_p}[\ul x]$. Denote the set of those $p$ by $S_K^{\prime\prime}$. For $p\in S_K^{\prime\prime}$, denote the number of $r$-tuples $\underline \omega \in \Ff_p^r$ such that $(\tilde P  \bmod \mathfrak{p})(\underline \omega)=0$ by $n_{\mathfrak{p}}(\tilde P)$. By the \emph{Lang-Weil estimate}, we have $n_{\mathfrak{p}}(\tilde P) = p^{r-1} + O( p^{r-3/2})$, and clearly we have $c_p(F) \ge n_{\mathfrak{p}}(\tilde P)$.
The \emph{Lang-Weil lower bound} from Section \ref{sec:motivation} follows (for every $p\in S_K^{\prime\prime}$).
Being more precise on the Chebotarev theo\-rem, the same argument leads to the stronger conclusion of Theorem \ref{th:onepoly} that the series
$\sum_{p\in \mathcal{P}} c_p(F)/p^r$ diverges. Indeed, the smaller series $\sum_{p\in S_K^{\prime\prime}} n_{\mathfrak{p}}(\tilde P)/p^r$
is of the same nature as $\sum_{p\in S_K^{\prime\prime}} 1/p$ (by the \emph{Lang-Weil estimate}); and we claim that
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim] We adjust an argument showing that the sum of inverse of primes $\leq n$ is asymptotic to $\log \log n$ when $n\rightarrow +\infty$.
For every integer $n\geq 0$, denote by $\pi_K(n)$ the number of primes $p\leq n$ that are in $S_K$. From the Chebotarev theorem,
the definition of the density and the prime number theorem, we have  $\pi_K(n) \simeq \gamma n/\log n$ when $n\rightarrow +\infty$.

From the effective form of Chebotarev proved by Lagarias-Odlyzko \cite{lagarias-odlyzko77} (and improved in \cite{serre-tchebotarev}), we have $\pi_K(n) = \frac{n}{\log n} \left( \gamma + O(\frac{1}{\log n})\right)$.
Claim (\ref{eq:chebotarev}) is the outcome of these evaluations:
where we bound $\sum_{k=3}^{n-1} \frac{1}{k \log k}$ by $\int_2^{n-1}  \frac{\dd x}{x \log x}$ and  $\int_3^{n}  \frac{\dd x}{x \log x}$ in the last step.

\begin{remark} If $F\in \Zz[\underline x]$ is irreducible in $\overline \Qq[\ul x]$, then the \emph{Lang-Weil estimate} gives that  $c_p(F)>0$ \emph{for all but finitely many} $p\in \mathcal{P}$. Thus polynomials $F\in \Zz[\ul x]$ like $F=x^2y^2+1$ for which $c_p(F)=0$ for infinitely many $p\in \mathcal{P}$ are necessarily reducible in $\overline \Qq[\ul x]$.

This section is devoted to \emph{systems} of polynomial equations. Our reduction to the situation of one equation is explained in Sections \ref{ssec:key_lemmas}--\ref{ssec:a_key_lemma}. The goal is Lemma \ref{lem:main}, which generalizes Lemma \ref{thm:reduction-intro} from Section \ref{sec:motivation}. Its applications, Corollary \ref{cor:cons2-intro} and Corollary \ref{cor:cons1-intro}, are then proved in Section  \ref{ssec:L-W} and Section \ref{ssec:cons1}. Section \ref{ssec:ostrowski} is a final illustration.
Fix the following for the whole subsection and the next one. Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $K$ be its fraction field.

\subsection{Proof of the Lang-Weil estimate assuming the case of hypersurfaces} \label{ssec:L-W}
We retain the notation and assumptions from Sections \ref{ssec:key_lemmas}--\ref{ssec:a_key_lemma}.
The \emph{hypersurface degree} of the $d$-dimensional affine variety $V\subset \Aa^r_R$ is defined to be the smallest degree of some polynomial $F\in K[\ul T,Y]$ such that
for some nonzero $c\in R$, the polynomial $F$ locally represents $V$ as a hypersurface over $R[c^{-1}]$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{def:def_hyp}). We denote it by $\hdeg(V)$.

\item If $R$ is integrally closed, we have $1\leq \hdeg(V) < +\infty$ (Lemma \ref{lem:exist_rep_hyp}). If $V$ is itself a hypersurface, then $\hdeg(V)\leq \deg(V)$ where $\deg(V)$ is the usual degree, i.e.{} the degree of a polynomial defining the hypersurface $V$. This inequality is strict in general: for example, the hypersurface $V\subset \Aa^2$ of equation $Y^2+T^4-2T^2Y-T=0$ can be represented by the hypersurface of equation $Y^2-T=0$ and so $\hdeg(V) \leq 2 < \deg(V) =4$.
\item The hypersurface degree is more intrinsic than the usual degree (which depends on the embedding $V\subset \Aa^r$): if $V_1\subset \Aa^{r_1}_R$ and $V_2\subset \Aa^{r_2}_R$ are
